Moving data

Sources & Sinks

A Source is pulled for Arrow batches until it says it has none left. A Sink is handed one batch and then closed.

In one line
How rows get into a Dataset and back out again
You need
The pcs-core/io feature for the traits, plus a connector crate for the transport and a transformer crate for the format
Read this if
Your Parquet file has an Int32 column where the component declares Int64, or your second run says write_batch called after finish

The shape of a drain cycle

Ingestion is pull: something calls next_batch() in a loop and appends each batch. Egress is push: something hands the sink a batch and then finalises it. Between the two sits the constraint that catches people out. A Dataset only accepts a batch whose schema matches the registered one exactly, so a cast usually has to happen first.

rows, batches, columns the registered schema

The two traits

Both live in pcs-core behind its io feature. Every implementation lives in a connector crate that depends on them. Each is a schema, a step, and a way to signal done.

Rustcrates/pcs-core/src/io/source.rs
#[async_trait]
pub trait Source: Send + Sync {
    /// Fixed per source instance — must not change between calls.
    fn schema(&self) -> Arc<Schema>;

    /// Pull the next batch, or `None` at EOF.
    async fn next_batch(&mut self) -> Result<Option<RecordBatch>, PcsError>;

    /// Progress reporting only. Callers must not rely on accuracy.
    fn estimated_rows(&self) -> Option<usize> { None }
}
Rustcrates/pcs-core/src/io/sink.rs
#[async_trait]
pub trait Sink: Send {
    /// May be called multiple times.
    async fn write_batch(&mut self, batch: &RecordBatch) -> Result<(), PcsError>;

    /// Flush and finalise. Exactly once, after the last batch.
    async fn finish(&mut self) -> Result<(), PcsError>;

    /// Batches must conform to this schema.
    fn schema(&self) -> Arc<Schema>;

    /// Backpressure probe. `None` if unsupported.
    fn pending_rows(&self) -> Option<usize> { None }
}

The bounds differ deliberately. Source is Send + Sync; Sink is only Send, because exclusive &mut self access already provides the synchronisation a writer needs. Concurrent writes to one sink are not a supported shape.

pending_rows is the only optional method with a real consumer: Pipeline::sink_pending_rows(component) surfaces it, and a BackpressureSpec::Predicate closure can consult it to skip a pipeline whose downstream sink is filling up. Of the built-in sinks, only ChannelSink implements it. A file sink has no meaningful queue depth.

Implementing a source is one method plus a schema:

Rustyield fixed-size chunks, then None
use std::sync::Arc;
use arrow_array::{Array, Float64Array, RecordBatch};
use arrow_schema::Schema;
use async_trait::async_trait;
use pcs_core::PcsError;
use pcs_core::io::Source;

struct RampSource {
    schema: Arc<Schema>,
    remaining: usize,
    chunk: usize,
}

#[async_trait]
impl Source for RampSource {
    fn schema(&self) -> Arc<Schema> {
        self.schema.clone()
    }

    async fn next_batch(&mut self) -> Result<Option<RecordBatch>, PcsError> {
        if self.remaining == 0 {
            return Ok(None);
        }
        let n = self.chunk.min(self.remaining);
        self.remaining -= n;

        let col: Arc<dyn Array> =
            Arc::new(Float64Array::from_iter_values((0..n).map(|i| i as f64)));
        RecordBatch::try_new(self.schema.clone(), vec![col])
            .map(Some)
            .map_err(|e| PcsError::generic(format!("RampSource: {e}")))
    }

    fn estimated_rows(&self) -> Option<usize> {
        Some(self.remaining)
    }
}

Aim for moderate batch sizes rather than one giant batch. The trait docs suggest around 64k rows. FileSource reads on a dedicated OS thread and hands batches over a tokio::sync::mpsc channel with capacity 4, so next_batch awaits instead of blocking the executor and the file is never fully materialised.

The batching contract

Two free functions do the driving. Note the argument order is not symmetric: the source comes first, the sink comes last.

Rustboth return the row count they moved
pub async fn drain_into_dataset<S: Source + ?Sized>(
    source: &mut S,
    dataset: &mut Dataset,
    component_name: &'static str,
) -> Result<usize, PcsError>;

pub async fn drain_dataset<K: Sink + ?Sized>(
    dataset: &Dataset,
    component_name: &'static str,
    sink: &mut K,
) -> Result<usize, PcsError>;
rows and batches who owns the loop

Three details matter. drain_dataset pulls the component's whole RecordBatch and issues a single write_batch, so a sink never sees the chunk boundaries the source produced. It returns Ok(0) without calling the sink at all when the component has no rows. And that batch is the raw one: soft-deleted rows are still in it, so call compact() before draining to keep them out of the output file.

Rustdriving both ends by hand
use std::path::Path;
use std::sync::Arc;
use pcs_connector_file::{FileSink, FileSource};
use pcs_core::Component;
use pcs_core::dataset::Dataset;
use pcs_core::io::{Sink, drain_dataset, drain_into_dataset};
use pcs_transformer_parquet::ParquetTransformer;

let mut data = Dataset::new();
data.register_component::<Trade>()?;

let parquet  = Arc::new(ParquetTransformer::new());
let mut src  = FileSource::open_async(Path::new("in.parquet"), parquet.clone(), None).await?;
let mut sink = FileSink::create_truncating(Path::new("out.parquet"), parquet, Trade::schema())?;

let rows_in = drain_into_dataset(&mut src, &mut data, "Trade").await?;
// ... run systems over `data` ...
let rows_out = drain_dataset(&data, "Trade", &mut sink).await?;
sink.finish().await?;

Or attach them to the pipeline and let it sequence the three phases for you:

Rustdrain sources, run systems, drain sinks, finish
let mut pipeline = Pipeline::builder("etl")
    .with::<Trade>()
    .with_source("Trade", src)
    .with_sink("Trade", sink)
    .with_parallel_system(ScaleSystem)
    .build();

pipeline.run_with_io().await?;
Sharp edge

run_with_io calls finish() on every registered sink at the end of every call. With a FileSink that makes it a one-shot API: the second call fails with FileSink: write_batch called after finish. For a long-running loop, drive the drains yourself. That is what run_standalone does, deferring finish() to the final iteration.

Sources are also drained one component at a time, each with its own row count. Two sources feeding two components with different numbers of rows will leave the Dataset inconsistent, because append_record_batch extends the shared row_count as it goes. Give every component the same number of rows per cycle, or drain only one.

Casting into the component schema

A component's schema is registered once and enforced on every append: the batch's schema().fields() must equal the registered fields(), compared by name, data type, nullability and order. There is no in-place retype of a registered column, so a cast is a pre-ingestion step. cast_batch is the pure function; CastingSource is that function wrapped as a Source.

RustCastOptions comes from the arrow-cast crate
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::path::Path;
use std::sync::Arc;
use arrow_cast::CastOptions;
use arrow_schema::DataType;
use pcs_connector_file::FileSource;
use pcs_core::io::{CastingSource, build_target_schema};
use pcs_transformer_csv::CsvTransformer;

// The file says Int32 / Float32; the component declares Int64 / Float64.
let csv  = Arc::new(CsvTransformer::new(true));   // true: the file has a header row
let file = FileSource::open(Path::new("trades.csv"), csv, Some(file_schema.clone()))?;

let mut overrides = HashMap::new();
overrides.insert("id",    DataType::Int64);
overrides.insert("price", DataType::Float64);
let target = build_target_schema(&file_schema, &overrides);

let src = CastingSource::new(file, target, CastOptions::default());

The rules cast_batch follows, in the order it applies them:

  • It walks the target's fields and looks each one up in the batch by name, so column order in the incoming batch does not matter.
  • A column in the batch that the target does not name is dropped.
  • A column the target names that the batch does not have is an error — cast_batch: source batch missing column '<name>'. A cast cannot invent data.
  • A column whose type already matches is cloned, not converted. Arrow arrays are reference-counted, so a matching cast costs nothing.
  • The result is rebuilt against the target schema exactly, which is why nullability comes from the target and the output is append-ready by construction.

CastOptions::default() is safe: true: a value that cannot be represented in the target type becomes null rather than an error. Set safe: false to get the error instead. The two settings interact. If safe mode produces a null for a field the target declares non-nullable, the rebuild fails with cast_batch: RecordBatch rebuild error.

build_target_schema(source, overrides) covers the common case: clone a source schema and replace the data type of a named subset of fields, keeping every field's nullability as it was.

Constraint

A cast adapts types, never shape. If the component declares a column the file does not contain, no CastingSource configuration will help; write a small wrapping Source that builds the missing array and re-assembles the batch. examples/connectors/scheduler_parquet_etl.rs does exactly that to pad a zero-filled output column.

What ships in the box

The traits, the two drain functions and the cast helpers live in pcs-core. The factory contract lives in pcs-connector. A connector crate carries bytes over one transport and a transformer crate turns bytes into batches, so a build pulls in parquet, arrow-csv or tokio-postgres only when it reads or writes that format.

WhatSourceSinkCargo feature
Traits & drains Source, Sink, drain_into_dataset, drain_dataset pcs-core/io (implies runtime)
Cast helpers cast_batch, CastingSource, build_target_schema pcs-core/io
Factory contract SourceFactory, SinkFactory, ConnectorContext, parse_schema_fields pcs-connector
Transformer contract Transformer, BatchReader, BatchWriter, MessageDecoder pcs-transformer
Channel ChannelSource ChannelSink pcs-connector-channel
File FileSource FileSink pcs-connector-file
PostgreSQL PostgresSource PostgresSink pcs-connector-postgresql
Kafka KafkaSource KafkaSink pcs-connector-kafka
NATS NatsSource NatsSink pcs-connector-nats
TCP TcpIngestSource TcpSink pcs-connector-tcp
HTTP HttpSource HttpSink pcs-connector-http
DataFusion SQL DataFusionSource — pcs-connector-datafusion
Config registration Registry, register_builtin_factories pcs-service/service

A format key names the transformer that turns a connector's bytes into batches, and one crate implements each name. The transformers page has the schema rules and the options each one takes.

formatTransformerCrate
csv CsvTransformer pcs-transformer-csv
ndjson NdjsonTransformer pcs-transformer-ndjson
parquet ParquetTransformer pcs-transformer-parquet
avro AvroTransformer pcs-transformer-avro
arrow-ipc ArrowIpcTransformer pcs-transformer-arrow-ipc

csv, ndjson, parquet and avro read and write a file stream. arrow-ipc has no stream surface, so it is a TCP, Kafka or NATS format, and ndjson and avro work in both places.

On the host side one pcs-service feature per crate decides what reaches the registry: connector-channel, connector-file, connector-http, connector-kafka, connector-nats, connector-postgresql, connector-tcp, transformer-arrow-ipc, transformer-avro, transformer-csv, transformer-ndjson and transformer-parquet. Each implies service, and service on its own registers nothing. connector-kafka and connector-nats pull in transformer-ndjson and connector-tcp pulls in transformer-arrow-ipc, their default formats. connector-file and connector-http pull in none: format is required there, so you pick.

DataFusionSource has no factory: it needs a live SessionContext, which a config file cannot express. Build it in Rust.

Every constructor, since they are not uniform:

Rustsignatures, not calls
// pcs-connector-file. open_async moves the open and the metadata read off the executor.
// create appends to an existing file, create_truncating replaces it.
FileSource::open           (&Path, Arc<dyn Transformer>, Option<Arc<Schema>>) -> Result<Self>
FileSource::open_async     (&Path, Arc<dyn Transformer>, Option<Arc<Schema>>) -> Result<Self>
FileSink::create           (&Path, Arc<dyn Transformer>, Arc<Schema>)         -> Result<Self>
FileSink::create_truncating(&Path, Arc<dyn Transformer>, Arc<Schema>)         -> Result<Self>

// pcs-connector-http. Neither makes a request: the source GETs and the sink
// sends on the first batch, so validate needs no reachable endpoint.
HttpSource::new(&str, Option<Arc<Schema>>, Arc<dyn Transformer>, Vec<(String, String)>, Duration) -> Result<Self>
HttpSink::new  (&str, Arc<Schema>, Arc<dyn Transformer>, method: &str, Vec<(String, String)>, Duration) -> Result<Self>

// The transformer each of those takes, one crate per format.
CsvTransformer::new(has_headers: bool)   -> Self   // csv
NdjsonTransformer::new(infer_max: usize) -> Self   // ndjson
ParquetTransformer::new()                -> Self   // parquet, Snappy
ArrowIpcTransformer::new()               -> Self   // arrow-ipc, messages only
AvroTransformer::new(compression: Option<CompressionCodec>, schema_id: Option<u32>) // avro

// pcs-connector-channel. Returns the paired endpoint alongside the source or sink.
ChannelSource::new(Arc<Schema>, buffer: usize) -> (mpsc::Sender<RecordBatch>, Self)
ChannelSink::new  (Arc<Schema>, buffer: usize) -> (Self, mpsc::Receiver<RecordBatch>)

Only ndjson infers a schema, and only when schema_fields is absent: csv requires one, and parquet and avro reject one, since the file carries its own. FileSource reports estimated_rows under parquet alone, summed from row-group metadata with no data read, and CastingSource forwards whatever it wraps. Every other source returns None.

finish() means different things per sink, and that matters when you decide where to call it. FileSink hands it to the transformer: parquet writes the footer and closes the writer, csv, ndjson and avro flush their buffered writer. After any of them a further write_batch is an error, and a second finish is a no-op. ChannelSink has nothing to flush.

The in-memory channel

ChannelSource and ChannelSink are a tokio mpsc pair dressed as IO. They exist for two jobs: testing a pipeline without touching the filesystem, and bridging a pipeline to another async task in the same process.

Rustthe sender and receiver are yours to hold
use pcs_connector_channel::{ChannelSink, ChannelSource};
use pcs_core::io::Source;

let (tx, mut src)   = ChannelSource::new(schema.clone(), 8);
let (mut sink, mut rx) = ChannelSink::new(schema.clone(), 8);

tx.send(batch).await.unwrap();
drop(tx);                                  // EOF: next_batch now returns Ok(None)

assert!(src.next_batch().await?.is_some());
assert!(src.next_batch().await?.is_none());

EOF is the sender being dropped, not a sentinel value, so a source you never drop the sender for will wait forever. ChannelSource validates each received batch against its declared schema and returns an error on mismatch, which makes it a useful place to catch a producer drifting from the component definition. ChannelSink clones each batch into the channel and reports pending_rows as configured capacity minus remaining capacity. Read that number carefully: an mpsc slot holds one RecordBatch, so it counts batches in flight, not rows, despite the method name.

One caveat if you reach these through the config file: ChannelSourceFactory and ChannelSinkFactory cannot hand the other endpoint back to you, so they build a pair whose sender is dropped immediately — an instant-EOF source. For real use, construct the channel yourself and pass the endpoint in programmatically.

SQL results as a Source

pcs-connector-datafusion adds one adapter, in one direction: a DataFusion query becomes a PCS Source. It streams lazily, pulling from DataFusion's execution stream one batch per next_batch, so a filter or aggregation runs in DataFusion and only the result crosses into the Dataset.

Rustfrom examples/connectors/datafusion_interop.rs
use datafusion::prelude::SessionContext;
use pcs_connector_datafusion::DataFusionSource;
use pcs_core::dataset::Dataset;
use pcs_core::io::drain_into_dataset;

let ctx = SessionContext::new();
ctx.register_table("sales", Arc::new(mem_table))?;

let mut src = DataFusionSource::from_sql(
    &ctx,
    "SELECT product_id, quantity, unit_price FROM sales WHERE region = 'north'",
).await?;

let mut data = Dataset::new();
data.register_raw_component("records", src.schema());
let rows = drain_into_dataset(&mut src, &mut data, "records").await?;

register_raw_component(name, schema) is the natural pairing here: the query's projected schema is only known after planning, so take it from the source rather than declaring a Component up front. DataFusionSource::from_stream takes a SendableRecordBatchStream you already hold, and with_estimated_rows(n) supplies the progress hint DataFusion cannot. estimated_rows is None otherwise.

There is no adapter in the other direction. A Dataset is not exposed as a DataFusion TableProvider. Run the example with cargo run -p pcs-connector-datafusion --example datafusion_interop.

Declaring IO in the config file

Every source and sink node is declared inside the one workflow block, and the service looks its type string up in a Registry of factories. That registry starts empty. Nothing is registered implicitly, so a config naming FileSource fails with no source factory registered for type until you install the connectors and the transformers.

Rustwith_runtime names the processor node the native pipeline fills
use pcs_service::service::builder::ServiceBuilder;
use pcs_service::service::factories::register_builtin_factories;

let builder = register_builtin_factories(ServiceBuilder::new())
    .with_runtime("enrich", Box::new(pipeline));
KDLcomponent names a component, not a file; transformer names a declared transformer node
workflow "trades" {
    transformer "pq" format="parquet"

    source "input" type="FileSource" component="Trade" transformer="pq" {
        config path="/data/trades.parquet"
    }

    wasm "enrich"

    sink "output" type="FileSink" component="Trade" transformer="pq" {
        config path="/data/out.parquet" {
            schema_fields "id" type="Int64" nullable=#false
            schema_fields "price" type="Float64" nullable=#false
        }
    }

    link from="input" to="enrich"
    link from="enrich" to="output"
}

A config node is opaque, handed straight to the factory, so the accepted keys are the factory's business. FileSource wants path, and takes schema_fields as the format dictates: required for csv, optional for ndjson, rejected for parquet and avro. FileSink always wants schema_fields: one node per column, named by its leading argument, where type is one of the Arrow primitive names (Int64, Float64, Utf8, Boolean, Date32 and so on) and nullable defaults to true. The channel factories accept buffer.

Byte format is a node property, not a config key. Each format the workflow needs is its own transformer node, whose options child reaches that format's factory: has_headers for csv, infer_max for ndjson, compression and schema_id for avro. Every source or sink that moves bytes names one by id through its own transformer key.

Two load-time gates then run before the first iteration. The workflow graph is validated inline as part of ServiceBuilder::build: every link must carry a component both ends agree on, with field-for-field identical Arrow schemas, and every component a processor declares must be delivered by some inbound link. A runtime that declares nothing opts its edges out of the component checks.

Cluster mode is narrower. It runs exactly one wasm or plugin node with no source, sink or link at all, because a cluster ingests through PartitionSource and a declared source would sit idle. That is a hard configuration error, not a warning.
